source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Oliver Mellors, to Connie and her sister Hilda

source.excerpt: “Well!” he said at last. “I agree to anything. The world is a raving idiot, and no man can kill it: though I’ll do my best. But you’re right. We must rescue ourselves as best we can.”
trail: Lawrence privately published the novel through the Tipografia Giuntina in Florence in 1928, after English publishers turned it down, per Wikipedia’s entry on the novel ↗.
The exact line appears in Chapter 18, spoken by gamekeeper Oliver Mellors right after Connie’s sister Hilda spells out the divorce plan — confirmed against the full chapter text at Wikisource ↗.
An unexpurgated edition of the novel wasn’t published openly in the UK until 1960, following the landmark obscenity trial, per the same Wikipedia account ↗.
The novel is now hosted as a public-domain text by Project Gutenberg ↗, which explicitly lists it as “Public domain in the USA.”
source.excerptNote: Mellors says this just after Hilda lays out the plan for the two divorces that would eventually let him and Connie marry.
source.rightsNote: Lady Chatterley’s Lover was first published in 1928, before the current U.S. public-domain cutoff of 1931, and Project Gutenberg lists its edition of the text as public domain in the USA.

author.heading: About D.H. Lawrence
author.bio: David Herbert Lawrence was an English novelist and poet whose work explored sexuality, industrialization, and emotional vitality, and repeatedly provoked censorship battles. Lady Chatterley’s Lover (1928), his final novel, was banned as obscene on first appearance and not published unexpurgated in Britain until 1960.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Mellors speaks this line late in the novel, as Connie’s sister Hilda spells out the elaborate legal maneuvering — two divorces, a manufactured co-respondent — needed before he and Connie could eventually marry. His weary “I agree to anything… though I’ll do my best” captures the novel’s central friction between individual desire and the rigid social and legal codes of the day.

The book itself became a real-world test of exactly the kind of censoriousness Mellors is grousing about: banned as obscene when it first appeared in 1928, it wasn’t legally published unabridged in Britain until Penguin’s acquittal in the famous 1960 obscenity trial.
